louise-bourgeois__hannah-arendt.text: Louise Bourgeois makes personal memory publicly accessible in rooms and things. Hannah Arendt asks how a common world can come into being between different people. A Cell does not simply convert private experience into shared knowledge. It places something between the viewers to which each person can build a relationship of their own.
louise-bourgeois__hannah-arendt.question: When does personal memory become part of a common world?

on-kawara__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins with the drawing of a boundary. Only through it do two sides come into being. On Kawara's date paintings rest on a similarly elementary distinction: this day and all other days. The boundary, however, is temporal. At midnight, today irrevocably becomes a yesterday. Kawara's rule of completing a painting only on the day it names makes this boundary materially effective. The date therefore does not merely designate a place in the calendar. It holds fast the moment at which a temporal distinction became irreversible.
on-kawara__george-spencer-brown.question: When does a boundary become past?

bruce-nauman__george-spencer-brown.text: Bruce Nauman repeats movements, gestures and sentences until the apparently identical produces differences. George Spencer-Brown describes form as the consequence of a distinction: a boundary separates two sides. Nauman's loops put a simple question to this notion. When the same movement begins again, is the same boundary drawn anew? Body, attention and moment have changed in the meantime. The form can recur, but the situation of its distinction cannot. Repetition would then be no circling within a fixed form, but a continued redrawing of its boundary.
bruce-nauman__george-spencer-brown.question: Can the same boundary be drawn twice?

dan-graham__michel-serres.text: Dan Graham builds boundaries of glass and mirrors that are interesting precisely because they do not simply close things off. They separate spaces and at the same time let light, gaze and reflection pass through. Michel Serres is interested in passages, and in the fact that mediation never remains neutral. Graham's glass wall is therefore boundary and channel at once. Whoever looks through it does not simply see the other side. Reflection, position and movement alter the relation between here and there. The boundary mediates precisely by separating.
dan-graham__michel-serres.question: When does a boundary become a channel?

dan-graham__elena-esposito.text: Dan Graham's time-delayed video makes the present visible only after it has passed. What I see on the monitor is what I have just done. While this image appears, the expectation of the next one is already forming. Elena Esposito examines how the future becomes effective in the present even though it has not yet occurred. Graham's delay generates exactly this tension: it continuously turns the present into past and thereby opens, at the same time, a horizon of what is about to appear. Here the future arises not despite the delay but through it.
dan-graham__elena-esposito.question: Does delay generate the future?

robert-smithson__george-spencer-brown.text: Robert Smithson's Site and Non-Site exist only through a distinction. Material is located in the exhibition space and at the same time refers to a place outside it. George Spencer-Brown shows that a boundary does not merely separate two sides, but first makes them determinable as sides of a form at all. With Smithson, it is precisely this separation that makes a shared address for something absent possible. Visitors need not enter the distant landscape together. They can refer to it in the museum because Site and Non-Site remain distinguished from and connected to each other.
robert-smithson__george-spencer-brown.question: Can a boundary make an absent place jointly accessible?

robert-smithson__gilbert-simondon.text: Robert Smithson's sites continue to change after an artistic decision has been made. Water, salt, weather and material carry on their history. Gilbert Simondon understands an individual not as a finished form but as the provisional state of an ongoing process. With Smithson, a simple question thereby becomes difficult: what exactly remains identical at a place? The location can be found again, its material condition cannot. Identity might therefore lie less in an unchanged state than in the continued history of a place.
robert-smithson__gilbert-simondon.question: How does a place remain the same when it changes?

eva-hesse__henri-bergson.text: Eva Hesse's materials age, sag, discolour and change their tension. Such changes can be documented as a sequence of individual states. Henri Bergson, however, warns against confusing time with a series of states laid side by side. Duration means that what is past continues to act in the present state. Hesse's material makes this thought almost physically visible. Today's latex does not replace yesterday's. Its present form has emerged from its history so far.
eva-hesse__henri-bergson.question: Can a material have duration?

on-kawara__hannah-arendt.text: On Kawara turns a single day into a lasting object. Hannah Arendt understands the common world as something that can exist between different people and outlast their respective lifetimes. Kawara's date painting, by contrast, begins with a radically personal now. It can come into being on this one day only. Once it is finished, however, precisely this past day can be viewed by many people at different times. A unique now thereby gains a place in a common world.
on-kawara__hannah-arendt.question: When does a single day become shared?

sol-lewitt__hannah-arendt.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions allow different people to execute the same work in different places. Hannah Arendt thinks of a common world not as agreement among all those involved, but as something to which people can refer from different positions. A Wall Drawing connects such positions in an unusual way. Those executing it need not see, think or do the same. Nevertheless their different actions refer to a common rule and bring forth a work that gains permanence between them.
sol-lewitt__hannah-arendt.question: Can a rule bring forth something shared?

tehching-hsieh__elena-esposito.text: At the start of a performance, Tehching Hsieh lays down what he will do for months or an entire year. A future not yet lived thereby already takes concrete form in the present. Elena Esposito examines how expectations and forecasts make what is to come effective without yet knowing it. With Hsieh, the rule is known, the future experience is not. Fatigue, illness, attention and lifetime have yet to occur. The contract describes a future and, precisely by doing so, already begins to organise the body now.
tehching-hsieh__elena-esposito.question: When does the future begin to act on a body?

james-turrell__elena-esposito.text: James Turrell builds situations in which seeing takes time. Eyes adapt, lighting conditions change, and a surface that at first seems empty can gradually gain depth. Elena Esposito examines how expectations make a future effective in the present. With Turrell, too, we therefore do not only see what is present at the moment. We wait for change, reckon with the next moment and direct our attention towards it. The future of seeing is already at work before anything new appears.
james-turrell__elena-esposito.question: When does expectation become part of seeing?

felix-gonzalez-torres__michel-serres.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres lets parts of his works leave the exhibition space. Paper is taken away, sweets are eaten and stocks are later replenished. Michel Serres is interested in passage, and in the fact that a transmission does not simply carry what is transmitted unchanged from one place to another. With Gonzalez-Torres, this change belongs to the identity of the work. It persists not despite its circulation but precisely through it.
felix-gonzalez-torres__michel-serres.question: Can passing something on preserve a form?

christian-marclay__hannah-arendt.text: Christian Marclay's The Clock joins thousands of film fragments into a time that coincides with the audience's clock time. Hannah Arendt describes a common world as something that exists between different people without making their perspectives the same. For this, Marclay provides an unusual common object. Different people see different images, sit in the room for different lengths of time and bring their own memories with them. Nevertheless, for a moment they find themselves in the same edited now.
christian-marclay__hannah-arendt.question: Can a shared present be cut together?

felix-gonzalez-torres__elena-esposito.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres defines works in such a way that their future states remain open. Sweets can disappear and be replenished, stacks of paper be depleted and renewed. Elena Esposito examines how the future is organised in the present without already being fixed. With Gonzalez-Torres, this openness belongs to the identity of the work. The work does not contain its next state, but rules for which changes it can survive in future as the same work.
felix-gonzalez-torres__elena-esposito.question: Does the future belong to the identity of a work?

william-kentridge__hannah-arendt.text: William Kentridge works with images in which political history does not appear closed. Drawings are erased and altered, while earlier states remain visible as traces. Hannah Arendt understands the common world as something that gains permanence between people and can at the same time be changed by their action. With Kentridge, the past is therefore neither removed nor simply preserved. It remains as the altered ground of present action. A common world has a history without being entirely determined by it.
william-kentridge__hannah-arendt.question: How much past does a shared future need?

doris-salcedo__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins with a boundary through which two sides come into being. Doris Salcedo works with cracks, blocked passages and things in which separation becomes physically palpable. With her, a boundary therefore does not appear as a neutral line. It can keep a past violence or an exclusion present. The space is divided, and precisely this division remains effective as a trace.
doris-salcedo__george-spencer-brown.question: Can a boundary remember?

louise-bourgeois__michel-foucault.text: With her Cells, Louise Bourgeois builds rooms in which seeing and access are precisely regulated. Michel Foucault examines arrangements according to how they distribute visibility and produce positions. With Bourgeois, one stands before grilles, doors and openings, looks in and at the same time remains outside. The Cell does not only show things. It organises from which point something becomes visible or hidden.
louise-bourgeois__michel-foucault.question: Who may see in a Cell and who remains outside?

on-kawara__lucy-suchman.text: On Kawara's date paintings follow a strict rule: the painting must be finished on the day it names. If this does not succeed, the rule cannot simply be continued the next day. Lucy Suchman shows that plans only become effective for action in concrete situations. With Kawara, the abstract order of the calendar therefore meets fatigue, working hours and midnight. The situation decides whether the plan becomes a work at all.
on-kawara__lucy-suchman.question: When does the situation decide about a rule?

bruce-nauman__michel-serres.text: Bruce Nauman lets movements, words and images return in loops. Michel Serres is interested in passage and in the disturbances that arise in the course of it. A loop seems at first to cancel every passage, since it arrives back at its beginning. Yet body, attention and meaning do not return unchanged. Each round carries something of the previous one with it and adds a new deviation.
bruce-nauman__michel-serres.question: Can a repetition return without disturbance?

felix-gonzalez-torres__hannah-arendt.text: Hannah Arendt links the common world to things that gain permanence between people. Felix Gonzalez-Torres creates works whose individual components, precisely, need not be permanent. Sweets are eaten, sheets taken away and later replaced. Nevertheless a work remains present to which different people can refer at different times. Duration lies here not in the individual thing but in a form maintained in common.
felix-gonzalez-torres__hannah-arendt.question: Can a transient work remain part of a common world?

william-kentridge__george-spencer-brown.text: William Kentridge draws figures, erases them and continues drawing on the same surface. George Spencer-Brown begins with a boundary through which a form first comes into being at all. With Kentridge, however, a boundary once drawn never disappears entirely. Erasing leaves shadows, smudges and residues that enter into the next drawing. The distinction can be cancelled without restoring an unmarked beginning.
william-kentridge__george-spencer-brown.question: What remains of an erased boundary?

tehching-hsieh__michel-foucault.text: Michel Foucault examines timetables, repetitions and controls as techniques through which bodies are ordered. Tehching Hsieh subjects himself to extreme rules over long periods. In the time clock performance, every hour becomes a prescribed position for the body. The decisive difference lies in the fact that this discipline is chosen as an artistic rule by the artist himself and made public. Precisely thereby its effect on everyday life becomes visible.
tehching-hsieh__michel-foucault.question: What happens when discipline is self-chosen?

dan-graham__gregory-bateson.text: Dan Graham's mirrors and video delays feed observations back into the situation from which they arose. Gregory Bateson is interested in feedback loops in which a result becomes the condition of the next step. With Graham, a person does not only see an image of themselves. This image changes how they go on moving and observing. Observation thereby becomes part of a circuit that continuously alters its own situation.
dan-graham__gregory-bateson.question: When does observation become feedback?

donald-judd__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins with a distinction that separates two sides from one another. Donald Judd's works make clear that the distance between things can accomplish such a separation too. The interval is not merely empty. It keeps bodies apart, determines their relation and gives rise to a sequence of individual forms. Without the distance, the elements would collapse into a different form.
donald-judd__george-spencer-brown.question: Can a distance generate a form?

bruce-nauman__gilbert-simondon.text: Gilbert Simondon understands individuation as a process in which an individual is not present as finished from the outset. Bruce Nauman repeats bodily movements until posture, rhythm and strain change. The instruction remains recognisable, yet with each pass the executing body becomes a different state of itself. Repetition stabilises the action and at the same time changes the one who performs it.
bruce-nauman__gilbert-simondon.question: Does the body become another through repetition?

james-turrell__gregory-bateson.text: Gregory Bateson describes information as a difference that makes a further difference. James Turrell works with lighting conditions in which the smallest changes become perceptible only after a while. A physical difference alone is therefore not enough. Body, adaptation and spatial context also decide whether it appears as a difference at all. Information arises here at the threshold of perception.
james-turrell__gregory-bateson.question: When does a difference in light become information?

william-kentridge__michel-foucault.text: Michel Foucault understands archives not as neutral stores of the past, but as orders under which something can become visible and sayable. William Kentridge takes up historical images, documents and political memories, redraws them and places them in new sequences. History thereby appears not as a finished stock. Its traces are rearranged and acquire different neighbours.
william-kentridge__michel-foucault.question: What history does a new order of traces generate?

tehching-hsieh__gilles-deleuze.text: Gilles Deleuze separates repetition from the mere occurrence of the same. Tehching Hsieh's rules drive this distinction to the extreme. In the time clock performance, formally the same action returns every hour, while body, fatigue and lifetime go on irrevocably. The strict sameness of the rule makes visible how different each single execution is.
tehching-hsieh__gilles-deleuze.question: How much difference does the same hour generate?

dan-graham__gilbert-simondon.text: Gilbert Simondon describes individuation as a process between individual and environment. Dan Graham's pavilions make such a relation immediately visible. Reflection, transparency and standpoint continuously alter what appears as observer, counterpart and environment. The viewing person does not simply stand before a finished situation. Their position arises anew, again and again, together with the spatial arrangement.
dan-graham__gilbert-simondon.question: Does an observer's position arise only in space?

donald-judd__jacques-derrida.text: Donald Judd separates bodies by precise distances and makes the interval an essential part of the work. Jacques Derrida uses the idea of spacing not only spatially. For him, identity also arises because something differs from other things and does not fully coincide with itself. Judd's intervals give this abstract difference a concrete spatial form.
donald-judd__jacques-derrida.question: Can an interval determine what a thing is?

bruce-nauman__claude-shannon.text: Claude Shannon separates the technical transmission of a message from its meaning. Bruce Nauman repeats words and sentences for so long that sound, rhythm and physical exertion can become more important than the original sense. The sequence of signs can remain almost the same while its effect shifts. A stable signal does not guarantee a stable meaning.
bruce-nauman__claude-shannon.question: Can the same message lose its meaning?

james-turrell__george-spencer-brown.text: George Spencer-Brown begins form with the drawing of a boundary. James Turrell shows how little is sometimes needed for this. An opening, an edge or a change of light zone can suddenly make a seemingly boundless field appear as form. The boundary adds no new object to the light. It makes visible a difference that without it would be perceived differently or not at all.
james-turrell__george-spencer-brown.question: When does a boundary turn light into form?

william-kentridge__michel-serres.text: Michel Serres is interested in translations and passages in which something does not survive the journey unchanged. William Kentridge lets drawing pass over into film, projection, theatre, music and movement. Each change of medium preserves something and at the same time alters rhythm, scale and perception. The work therefore has no neutral channel between its forms.
william-kentridge__michel-serres.question: What changes when the medium changes?

tehching-hsieh__claude-shannon.text: Tehching Hsieh's time clock performance generates an enormous sequence of clear time stamps. Claude Shannon could treat such distinguishable signs as transmissible information. Yet the stamp does not contain the fatigue, the lack of sleep or the lost freedom of movement that belong to its production. Hsieh makes visible how far a precise date can be from the time spent bodily.
tehching-hsieh__claude-shannon.question: How much life fits into a time stamp?

dan-graham__henri-bergson.text: Dan Graham's video delays divide time into precisely measurable seconds. Henri Bergson distinguishes such measurable time from lived duration. In front of the monitor the two meet. Ten seconds can be fixed with technical exactness, while the experience of seeing oneself again, belatedly, cannot be broken down into the same units. The measured delay produces a duration that passes differently from the clock.
dan-graham__henri-bergson.question: How long are ten seconds in perception?

donald-judd__hannah-arendt.text: Hannah Arendt gives the things of a common world their significance because they can gain permanence between different people. Donald Judd's objects are designed for durability, material and precise spatial relations. Viewers come and go, while the same bodies and distances become the point of reference again. The work connects different moments of perception through a relatively stable spatial order.
donald-judd__hannah-arendt.question: How does a thing establish shared duration?

bruce-nauman__susan-leigh-star.text: Susan Leigh Star examines infrastructures that remain invisible especially when they function smoothly. Bruce Nauman often makes the opposite out of an ordinary passage. Narrow corridors, cameras and spatial restrictions make width, access and control suddenly conspicuous. What otherwise merely makes the way possible becomes itself the object of perception.
bruce-nauman__susan-leigh-star.question: When does a passage become visible infrastructure?

james-turrell__susan-leigh-star.text: James Turrell's works can create the impression that light appears almost without mediation. Susan Leigh Star, by contrast, turns her gaze to the infrastructures that work in the background of an experience. Architecture, electricity, technical control and spatial shielding belong to the conditions of seeing with Turrell too. Precisely because they hardly attract notice, the light can appear so immediate.
james-turrell__susan-leigh-star.question: What has to work in the background for light to appear immediate?

william-kentridge__heinz-von-foerster.text: William Kentridge draws, erases and continues working on the remains of the previous drawing. Heinz von Foerster describes recursive processes whose results enter again into the conditions of the next operation. Kentridge's sheet works exactly like this, without becoming a closed circuit. Each new drawing responds to a surface that has already been altered by the previous one.
william-kentridge__heinz-von-foerster.question: When does an image begin to respond to its own history?

tehching-hsieh__michel-serres.text: Tehching Hsieh devises rules meant to hold, as far as possible without exception, over a long time. Michel Serres is interested in disturbance and in the fact that a channel often becomes visible precisely through its interruptions. With Hsieh, sleep, fatigue, illness and everyday life continually threaten the pure continuation of the rule. The possible disturbance therefore belongs to the performance, even though it is to be avoided.
tehching-hsieh__michel-serres.question: When does a disturbance make the rule visible?

mona-hatoum__gregory-bateson.text: Mona Hatoum makes boundaries physically palpable. Grilles, cages and familiar domestic forms can protect, confine or threaten at the same time. Gregory Bateson understands information not as an isolated thing but as a difference that becomes effective within a relation. A boundary therefore does not only separate two areas. It also changes which relations between them are possible. With Hatoum, it is precisely the separation that becomes the carrier of information about proximity, danger and belonging.
mona-hatoum__gregory-bateson.question: When does a boundary become information?

christian-marclay__george-spencer-brown.text: Christian Marclay joins sound, film and images through cuts. George Spencer-Brown likewise begins with a cut that brings forth the two sides of a form. But Marclay's montage shows a second movement: the same cut that separates fragments from one another is what makes their new connection possible in the first place. The boundary does not lie between connection and separation. It produces both at once. Montage would then be a form of joining that draws its force precisely from the visible interruption.
christian-marclay__george-spencer-brown.question: Does the cut connect because it separates?

mona-hatoum__michel-serres.text: Mona Hatoum's works turn doors, thresholds, grilles and everyday objects into uncertain transitions. Michel Serres is interested in passages and in the fact that transmission never simply leads from one side to the other. Whoever passes a boundary does not necessarily remain untouched by it. With Hatoum, the transition itself can become risky, electric, bodily or political. The boundary is then no quiet edge between two areas, but a place at which what is transmitted changes.
mona-hatoum__michel-serres.question: What happens to something when it passes a boundary?

william-kentridge__gilbert-simondon.text: William Kentridge draws, erases and continues drawing on the same surface. Earlier states do not disappear entirely, but remain effective as shadows and smudges. Gilbert Simondon understands individuation as an ongoing process in which an individual is never fully completed. Kentridge's image therefore has no identity behind its changes. It becomes this image precisely through them. The trace of a past state is not merely memory, but material for further individuation.
william-kentridge__gilbert-simondon.question: Can a trace remain part of identity?

agnes-martin__gilbert-simondon.text: Agnes Martin's grids appear stable, although their lines, intervals and surfaces are never perfectly identical. Gilbert Simondon thinks of individuals not as finished units but as provisional solutions within an ongoing process. Martin's order might therefore appear less as a rigid schema than as the continued individuation of a surface. Line by line, a unity arises whose identity is borne precisely by small deviations. The grid holds together without cancelling every difference.
agnes-martin__gilbert-simondon.question: How much deviation does a stable order need?

louise-bourgeois__gilbert-simondon.text: Louise Bourgeois returns again and again to rooms, body parts, parental figures and childhood memories. Gilbert Simondon would not understand identity as an unchanging core lying hidden behind such repetitions. Individuation goes on. Memory, too, would then not only be recourse to something fixed, but material for a later change. With Bourgeois, the past shapes new figures, while these figures in turn change how the past can become present.
louise-bourgeois__gilbert-simondon.question: Does memory become part of what we become?

felix-gonzalez-torres__susan-leigh-star.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres lets works shrink, be replenished, change location and still count as the same work. Susan Leigh Star shows that classifications and infrastructures in the background help decide what can be treated as the same object at all. With Gonzalez-Torres, the identity of the work is therefore not only an aesthetic question. Inventory, certificate, exhibition practice and institutional rules help to read change as continuation.
felix-gonzalez-torres__susan-leigh-star.question: Who decides when the work is still the same?

sol-lewitt__gregory-bateson.text: Sol LeWitt's instruction is at first information about a possible action. Gregory Bateson is interested in how information makes a difference only within relations and contexts. An instruction therefore cannot simply be transferred from the text to the wall. Those executing it must read, decide, measure and respond to the situation. Only in this chain does the rule become effective. The work arises not from information alone, but from information being translated into action.
sol-lewitt__gregory-bateson.question: What must a rule communicate in order to become effective?

sol-lewitt__claude-shannon.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions can be transmitted like messages. Claude Shannon asks how information passes through a channel, regardless of what it means. This is exactly where LeWitt becomes interesting. A brief instruction can suffice to bring forth very complex works in different places. Yet between transmitted information and visible work lie decisions, material and execution. The instruction can remain technically stable while its embodiment varies.
sol-lewitt__claude-shannon.question: How much information does a work need?

sol-lewitt__elena-esposito.text: Sol LeWitt's instruction exists before its concrete execution is visible. Elena Esposito examines how the future is structured in the present through expectations, programmes and decisions, without thereby already being fixed. LeWitt's rule does something similar. It limits the space of possible future images without anticipating every detail. The work is thus partly determined and partly still open. Its future is organised before it is executed.
sol-lewitt__elena-esposito.question: How open can a regulated future remain?

tehching-hsieh__gregory-bateson.text: Tehching Hsieh gives an everyday action a different meaning through a publicly fixed frame. Gregory Bateson also described communication in terms of frames that indicate how a behaviour is to be understood. A blow in play is something other than the same blow in a fight. Similarly, with Hsieh, the year-long contract changes what punching a clock, waiting or not speaking means. The rule does not only prescribe a sequence for the action. It marks the context in which each repetition becomes legible as part of the performance.
tehching-hsieh__gregory-bateson.question: What makes an action part of a performance?

sol-lewitt__michel-serres.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions travel between language, executing persons, wall, tool and space. Michel Serres is interested in passages in which transmission never remains entirely free of loss. Even a precise rule does not arrive at its destination unchanged. Scale, material and local decisions inscribe themselves into its execution. This does not mean that the instruction fails. Rather, its identity shows itself in the fact that it can pass through different translations.
sol-lewitt__michel-serres.question: Does an instruction remain the same along its way?

roman-opalka__george-spencer-brown.text: Roman Opalka sets number upon number, marking each time how far the sequence has already reached. George Spencer-Brown begins with a distinction that separates a marked from an unmarked area. With Opalka, beyond the last number written lies a continuation not yet carried out. With each new number this boundary shifts. What was just now the future of the series becomes its fixed past. Counting thus continuously generates a difference between already actualised and still open.
roman-opalka__george-spencer-brown.question: Where does the not-yet-counted begin?

marina-abramovic__claude-shannon.text: Marina Abramović can communicate the rules of a performance in a few sentences. Claude Shannon's information theory makes it possible to distinguish the transmission of such signs from their meaning. The rule can have arrived completely even though the event it triggers remains undetermined. Pain, hesitation, the audience's reaction and physical exhaustion are not contained in the message. Between transmissible instruction and lived execution a surplus opens up that does not disappear with more information.
marina-abramovic__claude-shannon.question: What does a completely transmitted rule lack?

mona-hatoum__henri-bergson.text: Mona Hatoum's boundaries are rarely mere lines in space. One has to avoid them, wait before them, approach them or put one's own body in relation to them. Henri Bergson distinguishes lived duration from a time that is broken down into individual measurable segments. Hatoum's boundary thereby acquires a temporal side. It is not only seen, but experienced in hesitating, circumventing and crossing. A spatial cut can continue as duration in the body.
mona-hatoum__henri-bergson.question: How long does a boundary last?

tehching-hsieh__george-spencer-brown.text: Tehching Hsieh's performances begin and end at precisely set points in time. George Spencer-Brown describes form as the result of a distinction between two sides. Hsieh's contract draws such a boundary right through the middle of life: inside and outside the performance, before and after. But the boundary does not stay at its beginning. It organises every following day. A cut once set begins to consume real lifetime.
tehching-hsieh__george-spencer-brown.question: When does a boundary begin to consume time?

christian-marclay__susan-leigh-star.text: Christian Marclay's montages presuppose that images and sounds can be found, stored and combined with one another. Susan Leigh Star examines infrastructures precisely where their work disappears behind the visible result. Behind a work like The Clock stand archives, formats, catalogues, playback technology and institutional procedures. The shared present in the exhibition space is carried by a vast invisible order. Montage therefore connects not only fragments, but infrastructures too.
christian-marclay__susan-leigh-star.question: What infrastructure holds a montage together?

hanne-darboven__george-spencer-brown.text: Hanne Darboven breaks time down into numbers, dates, lines and recurring operations of writing. George Spencer-Brown begins with the drawing of a distinction. A calendar, too, lives from a boundary being set between this day and the next. Darboven multiplies such cuts until a visible order arises from them. Time thereby appears at once as continuous passing and as a sequence of artificially set differences.
hanne-darboven__george-spencer-brown.question: What does the cut between two days generate?

mona-hatoum__gilles-deleuze.text: Mona Hatoum repeats familiar forms such as cage, map, bed or household appliance, but changes scale, material or function. Gilles Deleuze understands repetition not as the return of the identical, but as the production of difference. Precisely for this reason Hatoum's boundaries become unstable. The recurring form does not confirm what a boundary is. It shifts its meaning from protection to threat, from home to exclusion, from order to insecurity.
mona-hatoum__gilles-deleuze.question: What does repetition change about a boundary?

mona-hatoum__jacques-derrida.text: Mona Hatoum's grilles, maps and domestic forms can take on entirely different meanings in different contexts. Jacques Derrida links repeatability to the possibility that a sign is detached from its original context and read differently. A boundary, too, therefore does not remain identical merely because its form recurs. The same fence can mean protection, captivity or political division. Repetition preserves the form and at the same time shifts its legibility.
mona-hatoum__jacques-derrida.question: Can the same boundary remain the same in another place?

sol-lewitt__gilles-deleuze.text: Sol LeWitt's rules are repeatable, yet their executions do not entirely coincide. Gilles Deleuze is interested precisely in a repetition that brings forth difference. With LeWitt, this difference does not lie outside the rule. It arises through its renewed application to other walls, dimensions, materials and situations. That an instruction can be repeated therefore guarantees no identical results. The rule produces a family of related but not identical events.
sol-lewitt__gilles-deleuze.question: How much difference can the same rule bear?

sol-lewitt__heinz-von-foerster.text: Sol LeWitt often lays down rules by which a sequence of decisions or operations is carried out. Heinz von Foerster is interested in recursion, when results enter again into later operations. Not every LeWitt rule is recursive. But where a line once set changes the conditions for the next, the instruction tips from mere repetition into a process with memory. What has already been executed becomes the precondition of the further course.
sol-lewitt__heinz-von-foerster.question: When does a rule acquire a memory?

sol-lewitt__jacques-derrida.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions can be executed again in different places and at different times. Jacques Derrida calls this repeatability iterability. A sign must be able to be detached from its original context in order to be repeatable at all. But precisely thereby its context changes. LeWitt's rule remains recognisable because it can be repeated, and each repetition at the same time exposes it to other spatial and material conditions.
sol-lewitt__jacques-derrida.question: Can a rule be repeated identically?

felix-gonzalez-torres__n-katherine-hayle.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres separates the identity of a work from an unchanging material stock. Sweets disappear, paper is taken away and later replaced. N. Katherine Hayles criticises the notion that information can be fully detached from its embodiment. Exactly this tension sustains Gonzalez-Torres' works. The rule or the certificate alone is not the work, but no single material state suffices either. Identity is distributed between information and ever new embodiment.
felix-gonzalez-torres__n-katherine-hayle.question: Where does the identity of a materially changing work reside?

sol-lewitt__henri-bergson.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions can break a procedure down into individual steps. Henri Bergson warns against confusing lived time with a series of units laid side by side. Whoever executes a Wall Drawing experiences both at once. The rule orders what is to happen one after another, while the work is experienced as indivisible duration. Planning can structure time, but it does not contain the time its execution actually takes.
sol-lewitt__henri-bergson.question: Can an instruction order duration?

tehching-hsieh__heinz-von-foerster.text: Tehching Hsieh's long-term performances rest on recurring actions. Heinz von Foerster describes recursion as the feeding back of a result into the conditions of the next operation. With Hsieh, too, the next repetition is never entirely without preconditions. Fatigue, missed sleep and the time already passed change the body that has to fulfil the rule once more. The rule remains the same, while its own execution continuously generates new conditions.
tehching-hsieh__heinz-von-foerster.question: What does each repetition change about the next?

felix-gonzalez-torres__karen-barad.text: Felix Gonzalez-Torres' works come into being in an arrangement of material, exhibition space, rules and actions of the audience. Karen Barad calls relations in which the sides involved are not already fully fixed beforehand intra-actions. A pile of sweets is therefore not simply a finished work with which visitors subsequently do something. Taking and replenishing belong to the conditions under which its respective state and its identity are brought forth.
felix-gonzalez-torres__karen-barad.question: Who or what produces the work in each case?

rebecca-horn__gilbert-simondon.text: Rebecca Horn connects bodies with feathers, rods, masks and mechanical extensions. Gilbert Simondon thinks of individuation as a process between an individual and its milieu. Horn's apparatuses therefore leave open where the finished body is supposed to begin. New reaches, resistances and movements arise only in the connection. The machine does not simply supplement an already completed organism. Body and apparatus determine themselves anew in their interplay.
rebecca-horn__gilbert-simondon.question: Where does the body end when the apparatus comes into being with it?

marina-abramovic__gilles-deleuze.text: Marina Abramović has repeated her own performances and re-performed historical performances by other artists. Gilles Deleuze understands repetition not as identical return, but as the production of difference. This becomes especially clear with performance. The same sequence meets a different body, a different audience and a different historical situation. Re-performance preserves a form only by bringing forth a new event.
marina-abramovic__gilles-deleuze.question: Can a performance recur without becoming the same?

sol-lewitt__michel-foucault.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions seem at first only to lay down what is to be executed. Michel Foucault directs attention to how rules at the same time organise positions, responsibilities and visibility. A Wall Drawing makes certain forms visible, while the work of those executing it easily disappears behind the artist's name and the apparent neutrality of the rule. The instruction therefore orders not only lines, but also roles in the process of production.
sol-lewitt__michel-foucault.question: Who becomes visible through a rule?

marina-abramovic__heinz-von-foerster.text: Marina Abramović's performances can create situations in which the observers do not remain outside what is happening. Heinz von Foerster's second-order cybernetics directs attention to the observer as part of what is observed. A glance, an approach or a withdrawal by the audience changes the situation, which is then responded to in turn. Observation thereby acquires consequences and returns to the performance as an altered condition.
marina-abramovic__heinz-von-foerster.question: What happens when observation acts back?

marina-abramovic__jacques-derrida.text: Marina Abramović ties performance to the presence of a body in an unrepeatable present. Jacques Derrida makes visible at the same time that an event can only be passed on if traces of it become repeatable. Photographs, descriptions, videos and reenactments do not rescue the original presence. They create new situations in which the past event returns differently. Precisely the uniqueness of the performance thus produces the conditions of its later repetition.
marina-abramovic__jacques-derrida.question: What remains of a unique present?

sol-lewitt__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.text: Sol LeWitt's instruction is repeatable without every execution having to be identical. Wendy Hui Kyong Chun describes digital media in terms of repetition, habit and update: something remains functional by being renewed again and again. LeWitt's rule can be read similarly. It does not preserve a finished state, but enables new actualisations of the same work. Stability arises from the capacity to be executed again.
sol-lewitt__wendy-hui-kyong-chun.question: When does a rule become an update?

tehching-hsieh__judith-butler.text: Tehching Hsieh subjects himself to an explicitly formulated rule whose repetition orders his behaviour over months or years. Judith Butler, by contrast, examines norms that are often effective precisely because they do not lie before us like rules. They become self-evident through repeated actions. Hsieh's performance makes this difference visible: his rule is artificial, dated and terminable, yet its continued execution begins to structure everyday life and body like a norm.
tehching-hsieh__judith-butler.question: When does a rule begin to act like a norm?

sol-lewitt__donna-haraway.text: Sol LeWitt's instructions can give the impression that a rule is independent of who executes it. Donna Haraway contradicts the notion of a knowledge without standpoint. Even the most precise instruction is read, measured out and implemented by particular bodies in particular places. Differences in space, material and experience do not disappear behind the rule. The seemingly general instruction receives a concrete, situated form every time.
sol-lewitt__donna-haraway.question: From what place is a rule executed?

agnes-martin__george-spencer-brown.text: Agnes Martin's lines divide the picture surface, yet their effect depends heavily on distance, light and attention. George Spencer-Brown begins form with the drawing of a distinction. What is interesting with Martin is how little such a distinction needs. A barely visible line can generate two areas, but only for a gaze that perceives it at all. Boundary and observation arise here almost in the same moment.
agnes-martin__george-spencer-brown.question: When does a line become a boundary?

marina-abramovic__michel-foucault.text: Marina Abramović often exposes bodies to conditions that are publicly observable. Michel Foucault examines visibility not merely as seeing, but as a component of arrangements in which behaviour is guided and judged. In a performance, the audience therefore does not only change the attention. Its presence belongs to the situation in which endurance, rule-following and transgression acquire meaning. The gaze is no invisible outside, but a condition of the execution.
marina-abramovic__michel-foucault.question: When does visibility become part of the action?

bruce-nauman__lucy-suchman.text: Bruce Nauman develops simple tasks, movements and spatial arrangements that quickly become more complicated in execution. Lucy Suchman shows that a plan does not fully contain an action. Bodies have to respond to space, resistance, balance and unexpected situations. Nauman's repetitions make exactly this difference visible. The instruction remains brief, while each execution demands new small decisions.
bruce-nauman__lucy-suchman.question: What remains of a plan in the body?

tehching-hsieh__donna-haraway.text: Tehching Hsieh's time rules seem at first entirely general: an hour is sixty minutes for everyone. Donna Haraway reminds us that all knowledge and all experience is situated. For Hsieh's body, the same hour means something different depending on sleep, fatigue, weather and what has gone before. The clock establishes equality while the body experiences difference. Precisely this tension makes measurable time visible as a concrete condition of life.
tehching-hsieh__donna-haraway.question: Whose time does the same clock measure?

doris-salcedo__michel-foucault.text: Doris Salcedo works with material traces of violence and loss without simply replacing the absent with images. Michel Foucault examines orders of visibility and the conditions under which something can appear. Salcedo's works therefore do not merely exhibit memories. They organise a form of seeing in which gap, empty place and damaged material become legible. Absence becomes visible without thereby being cancelled.
doris-salcedo__michel-foucault.question: How does absence become visible without being cancelled?

james-turrell__lucy-suchman.text: James Turrell plans rooms, openings and lighting conditions with great precision. Lucy Suchman shows, however, that planned procedures only become actual actions in concrete situations. Perception, too, cannot be fully pre-programmed. Eyes adapt at different speeds, people move, wait or overlook something. Turrell can design conditions of seeing, but not the individual act of seeing itself. The work therefore arises between spatial planning and situated execution.
james-turrell__lucy-suchman.question: Can perception be planned?
